props.title: Gordon's War

sections.content: Gordon's War (1973) exemplifies the gritty, street-level action films that dominated Black cinema in the early 1970s. Following Vietnam veteran Gordon Hudson's violent crusade against Harlem drug dealers, it shares thematic DNA with Shaft (1971) and Super Fly (1972), but takes a darker, more politically charged approach. Director Ossie Davis crafts a raw urban narrative that reflects the real concerns of Black communities dealing with heroin epidemics and police corruption, while delivering intense action sequences that influenced later vigilante films like Death Wish (1974).

sections.content: The film's Vietnam veteran angle tapped into a crucial cultural moment, as Gordon's War was among the first to explore Black veterans' experiences returning home to find their communities ravaged by drugs and corruption. This theme would later be expanded in films like Dead Presidents (1995) and Da 5 Bloods (2020). The tactical military training sequences and urban warfare strategies Gordon employs were innovative for the era, influencing later action films about veterans like First Blood (1982).

Director Ossie Davis brings documentary-style realism to the streets of Harlem, shooting on location with a mix of professional actors and local residents. This approach aligned with other socially conscious Black films of the period like The Spook Who Sat by the Door (1973) and Three the Hard Way (1974), which balanced entertainment with political commentary about systemic racism and community empowerment. sections.content: While often categorized as blaxploitation, Gordon's War helped establish conventions of the urban vigilante film that would define much of 1970s cinema. Its influence can be seen in later films like Vigilante (1982) and The Exterminator (1980), which similarly featured Vietnam veterans taking the law into their own hands. The film's unflinching portrayal of street violence and corruption also paved the way for grittier crime dramas like Ms. 45 (1981) and Fighting Back (1982).
